planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; the marbled white variegation on Alaska's leaves is genetically stable and shows from the seedling stage on, making it easy to spot in a mixed planting.

directions: Direct sow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; rich soil pushes leafy growth at the expense of bloom. Alaska is a classic compact, mounding nasturtium grown as much for its striking foliage as its flowers, with round leaves heavily marbled and streaked in creamy white over green, giving the plant strong ornamental value even before it flowers. It produces the same bright mix of cream, yellow, orange, and red single blooms typical of nasturtiums, and the variegated leaves make an especially attractive edible garnish alongside the peppery flowers. Its compact habit suits containers, edging, and small beds, and plants bloom continuously from early summer through frost with minimal care.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; unlike compact bedding nasturtiums, Moonlight is a true climbing type and needs a trellis, fence, or nearby shrub to scramble up.

directions: Direct sow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun at the base of a trellis, fence, or arbor, since Moonlight is a vigorous climbing nasturtium capable of scrambling 6 to 8 feet by twining leaf stems rather than tendrils. Its soft, pale primrose-yellow flowers glow in evening light, giving the variety its name, and provide a gentler color note than the hot oranges and reds of most nasturtiums. As with other nasturtiums, keep soil on the lean side, since overly rich soil produces abundant foliage but fewer flowers, and both leaves and blooms are edible with the characteristic peppery, watercress-like bite. Plants bloom from early summer until frost and make an easy, fast-growing vertical accent for a vegetable garden trellis or fence line.
